dek: SpaceX thrusters let it hover, spin, and land, but it won't ship until 2028.

slides.label: What Happened
slides.text: Tesla revealed its redesigned second-gen Roadster at an event outside Waco, Texas, powered by *SpaceX thrusters*.

slides.label: The Demo
slides.text: Using thrusters, the Roadster drove up an inverted ramp, spun, landed, and even *lifted itself over* a Cybertruck and Model Y mid-drive.

slides.label: The Numbers
slides.text: Tesla says it hits *0 to 60 mph in under one second*, tops 230+ mph, and gets 300 miles of range.

slides.label: Three Trims
slides.text: Performance ($50K to reserve), Thrust ($250K to reserve), and Rocket (invite-only, 10 thrusters, seats one).

slides.label: How It Works
slides.text: 10 thrusters tap *600 liters of compressed air* stored in pressure vessels packed into 'every usable void' in the car.

slides.label: The Design
slides.text: Angular, stark white body inspired by the *SR-71 spy plane*, F-35 jet, and Musk's own Bond-film Lotus Esprit.

slides.label: Years in the Making
slides.text: First teased in 2017, delayed five times since. Musk now says *production starts in 2028*, no price confirmed.

slides.label: Why It Matters
slides.text: Flashy halo cars dominate the spotlight, but real innovation access for *underrepresented founders* in auto and aerospace still needs funding, not hype.

caption_instagram:
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster, and yes, this SpaceX-powered car can actually fly. Elon Musk showed off the vehicle at an event outside Waco, Texas, where it drove up an inverted ramp, spun midair, and landed itself using 10 cold-gas thrusters.

The specs are wild: 0 to 60 mph in under one second, speeds past 230 mph, and 300 miles of range across all three trims. Reserve the base 'Performance' trim for $50,000, 'Thrust' for $250,000, or wait for an invite to the single-seat 'Rocket' trim.

But don't get too excited yet. Tesla first teased this car back in 2017 and has delayed it five separate times since. Musk now says production starts in 2028, nearly a decade after it was first promised, according to TechCrunch.

caption_linkedin:
Tesla's redesigned second-generation Roadster, unveiled this week with SpaceX-built thrusters, is a lesson in managing a product timeline (or not).

First shown in 2017 with a promised few-years delivery, the car has now been delayed five times. Elon Musk says production finally starts in 2028, nine years after that original promise, according to TechCrunch.

For founders, the takeaway isn't the thrusters or the 0-to-60 numbers. It's the gap between hype and delivery. Tesla can absorb nearly a decade of delays because of its scale, cash, and brand loyalty. Most founders, especially underrepresented ones building in hardware or deep tech, don't get that runway. Investors and customers expect delivery dates to mean something.

The Roadster will reportedly start at $50,000 just to reserve, with a 'Rocket' trim that's invite-only. Flashy halo products can build brand equity, but they also set a standard for what 'on time' looks like in tech.

Would you bet on a product with a nine-year delay track record? Yes or no.
